etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English chek, chekke, borrowed from Old French eschec, eschek, eschac, from Medieval Latin scaccus, borrowed from Arabic شَاه (šāh, “king or check at chess, shah”), borrowed from Classical Persian شَاه (šāh, “king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (mlkʾ /⁠šāh⁠/), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšáyati (“he rules, he has power over”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tek- (“to gain power over, gain control over”).

Compare Saterland Frisian Schak, Schach, Dutch schaak, German Schach, Danish skak, Swedish schack, Icelandic skák, French échec, Italian scacco. Doublet of chess and shah (“king of Persia or Iran”), from the same source, as well as thig, which derives from the Germanic cognate.

All of the English senses developed from the chess sense. The sense "financial instrument" derives from the sense of "means of verification" (i.e. against forgery), likely influenced by the already related word exchequer.
senses: A control; a limit or stop.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English chekken, partly from Old French eschequier and partly from the noun (see above).
senses: An expression showing that a requirement has been satisfied.
An expression that indicates that the speaker wishes to pay the bill (e.g. in a restaurant).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
paragraphs: By shortening from chequer, from Old French eschequier (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium, ultimately from the same Persian root as above.
senses: (textiles, chiefly in the plural) A pattern made up of a grid of squares of alternating colors; a checkered pattern.
Any fabric woven with such a pattern.
(transitive) To mark with a check pattern.
(heraldry, rare, possibly only as a printing error) Checky, i.e. chequy.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
senses: (India, Pakistan) Alternative form of chick (“window blind or door screen”).
